Wel@ome back! Part One of the Lifetime Repertoire:
King’s Indian Defense dealt with White’s most straightforward route:
developing the pieces and taking control of the centre. I hope I did a good
job convincing you that Black’s position is fully playable there, both
objectively fine and giving us great chances practically. It’s not
surprising that many players would never dream of entering the Mar del Plata
on the White side, and instead go for an early deviation. I should just say at
this point that you don’t need to have studied part one for this course to
be of benefit. There are a few transpositions in the opening chapters, but
these can be studied either way around. You may already have lines you’re
happy with against the Classical and Samisch Variations, or you might be
concerned by an early White sideline, in which case it would make sense to
start with part two.Here we’ll examine all of White’s other approaches. We
start with a few topical tries where White delays developing their king’s
knight: 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.e4 d6 5.Be2 White’s idea is generally to play g2-g4,
making it harder for our traditional ...f7-f5 counter. This is very ambitious
but fraught with danger. White’s king will no longer feel safe on the
kingside and often remains in the centre. White needs to keep absolute control.
A single misstep and his entire position collapses.We’ll move on to some
setups where White puts his bishop on g5. 5.Bg5 The point of this is to make
it harder for us to play ... e7-e5 due to the pin on our queen. However, by
developing the bishop a bit prematurely White has weakened his queenside, and
so opening up the long diagonal with 5...c5 , and a transposition into Benoni
setups works very well. We often reach positions where White’s prospects
would be much improved if he could place his bishop back on c1.Next up we
defang the Four Pawns Attack. îîStartFENîîrnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/2PPP3/2N5/
PP3PPP/R1BQKBNR w KQkq - 0 5îîEndFENîî 5.f4 Thanks to its name this variation
appeals to aggressive-minded players, but White actually has to show a lot of
accuracy to keep his centre together. I’ll demonstrate that the e4-pawn is
too weak, and with pawn and even piece sacrifices we’ll demolish White’s
big centre, leaving him with just holes.After investigating a few slightly
rarer setups:  • The Seirawan Variation: ��StartFEN��rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/

ppppppbp/5np1/8/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPPP/R1BQKBNR w KQkq - 2 4îîEndFENîî 4.Nf3 O-O 5.
Bg5 It’s on to the most theoretical section of this course: the Fianchetto
Variation: 3.g3 . By copying our kingside fianchetto White isn’t interested
in attempting to refute our setup. Instead, he tries to keep as much control
as possible and wants to prevent our famed activity. Don’t worry, we’ll
still get double-edged exciting positions. I propose playing with ...d7-d6 and
...c7-c5: 3...Bg7 4.Bg2 O-O 5.Nc3 d6 6.Nf3 c5 This is quite a rare setup, but
one in which I’ve had very good results. We offer White a transposition to
the Fianchetto Benoni, but bypass White’s critical option. In fact, with our
move order wrinkle, we’ll really annoy those who used Boris Avrukh’s
series of books to create a repertoire. Our idea is unmentioned and so our
opponents are bound to panic!A big advantage of the King’s Indian is its
flexibility. Not only have I covered all White’s tries against the King’s
Indian, but I’ve built a complete repertoire against everything except 1.e4.
A lot of players are too scared to allow us to enter the pure King’s Indian.
I hope after going through this course you’ll no longer be annoyed by the
London System but agree with me that Black’s position has dynamic potential
and is much the easier to play. Englishes and Retis won’t worry us in the
slightest, and neither will offbeat first moves like Adhiban’s 1.b3. I’m
recommending 1...Nf6 and 2...g6 against almost everything.The big exception is
when White plays an early Nc3 with the pawn remaining on c2. Here I recommend
playing ...d7-d5 to prevent White from transposing into a Pirc. With White’s
c-pawn blocked there’s no transposition into usual Queen’s Gambit style
positions, and we’ll quickly seize the initiative with a quick ...c7-c5
ourselves.This second part of the repertoire ended up being quite large, but I
hope you’ll agree with me that Black’s play is quite logical, making it
easier to remember. Working through the course will be a worthwhile investment.
Not only will you have a dynamic and sound repertoire where you can fight for
the win, but playing will actually be fun!
